# Two opposite double cores force a quadrilateral at a strict-excess minimum

This is a bounded ordinary planar reduction. It does not assert that every inverse-chord minimum is a triangle or even that every minimum falls in the case treated below.

Use the six endpoints and areas from `candidate 83b3822a403eee2c`:

    R=(A,B,t,a,b,r),
    W=(Y_3,X_2,Y_1,X_3,Y_2,X_1).

All radii and sector areas are positive. Consider the objective

    lambda=1/[1+(B+b)/(A+a)+(B+b)/(r+t)].                  (1)

Allow arbitrary constraints depending only on the six sector areas. In particular these may include the cap ceiling, total-area normalization, and sorted cap profile. A finite-data local minimum means a local minimum among actual feasible endpoint/area data in the ordinary Euclidean topology of these twelve positive parameters. An attained global minimum over actual bodies is sufficient. No assertion about a Hausdorff-local minimum of a given body is needed.

**Theorem.** Suppose such a minimum satisfies

    Y_3=AB/2,       Y_2=br/2,                            (2)

while the other four sectors have strictly positive excess over their core areas:

    X_2>Bt/2, Y_1>at/2, X_3>ab/2, X_1>Ar/2.            (3)

Then the actual realizing body is a quadrilateral. Its four vertices lie respectively in the interiors of sectors `X_2,Y_1,X_3,X_1`. The prescribed six chord endpoints all lie in relative interiors of its edges. The actual body is uniquely determined by these endpoint/area data.

The proof retains both PSD blocks and actual-body rigidity. Additional core equalities, including `Y_1=at/2`, are outside (3) and require separate analysis.

## 1. Both PSD blocks must be singular

Write the exact sector matrix as

    L_ii=1/(2W_(i-1))+1/(2W_i)-1/R_i^2,
    L_(i,i+1)=1/(2W_i)-1/(R_i R_(i+1)).                  (4)

The two zero-excess sectors (2) make edges `0--1` and `4--5` of this matrix zero. The matrix is the direct sum of a two-node block on `{5,0}` and a four-node block on `{1,2,3,4}`. By (3), every internal off-diagonal entry of these two path blocks is strictly negative.

Suppose first that the two-node block is positive definite. Decrease A slightly and increase B to maintain `AB=2Y_3`, leaving all areas and all other radii fixed. The two-node block changes continuously, so it remains positive definite for a sufficiently small change. In the four-node block, only B changes. Its diagonal and its adjacent off-diagonal entry both increase. The latter stays negative because `X_2>Bt/2` initially; taking a sufficiently small change preserves this strict core inequality. The four-node block therefore stays positive semidefinite by entrywise domination on nonnegative vectors and the Z-matrix absolute-value argument. The separating zero edge remains zero exactly. Every other core inequality is unchanged or retains its strict slack.

Thus the changed data are actually realizable by the exact PSD theorem. Their target chord increases while the chord `A+a` decreases. Formula (1) strictly decreases, contradicting local minimality. The two-node block must be singular.

Next suppose the four-node block is positive definite. Decrease t slightly, fixing all other radii and all areas. This alters only the four-node block, which remains positive definite by openness. Both affected core products `Bt,at` decrease, so core feasibility persists. The two-node block is unchanged. Exact PSD realization again gives an actual feasible body, now with `r+t` strictly smaller and both other chord lengths fixed. Formula (1) strictly decreases. Hence the four-node block is singular as well.

These are finite, sufficiently small changes of the actual data. There is no assumption that an arbitrary limiting body or selected center converges, and no omitted boundary mode: strictness in (3) supplies the needed slack before each perturbation.

## 2. The reciprocal charges and all six straight joins are forced

For completeness, use the exact charge notation

    D_i=R_i R_(i+1),
    h_i=1/D_i-1/(2W_i)>=0,
    b_i=(D_(i-1)+D_i-R_(i-1)R_(i+1))/(D_(i-1)D_i).

For any feasible polygonal replacement the positive edges have charges r_i,s_i with

    r_i s_i/(r_i+s_i)=h_i,
    delta_i=b_i-r_(i-1)-s_i>=0.                         (5)

Zero edges have both charges zero. The exact Gram identity is

    x^T L x=sum_i delta_i x_i^2
       +sum_(h_i>0)(s_i x_i-r_i x_(i+1))^2/(r_i+s_i).   (6)

Each singular connected path block with strictly negative edges has a positive kernel vector, unique up to scale. An elementary proof is to minimize the Rayleigh quotient, replace a minimizer by its coordinatewise absolute value, and use the eigenvector equation to propagate any zero coordinate to every adjacent coordinate; this rules out zeros. For any positive kernel vector w, another kernel vector x satisfies the identity

    x^T L x=sum_(edges i,j) h_ij w_i w_j
                        (x_i/w_i-x_j/w_j)^2,

obtained by using `Lw=0` in the diagonal terms. Connectedness proves that the kernel is one-dimensional.

Apply (6) to a positive kernel vector on each of the two singular blocks, extended by zero elsewhere. Every node belongs to one such block, so every `delta_i` is zero. On each positive edge, `s_i w_i=r_i w_(i+1)`, which determines its two charges uniquely using (5). The arbitrary scale of a block kernel cancels. Thus all positive-edge charges, and hence all inserted sector vertices, are uniquely fixed. On a zero edge the sector is the core triangle and has no new extreme vertex.

The equality `delta_i=0` is exactly equality in the prescribed-endpoint convexity constraint. In the exact sector replacement this means the two boundary segments meeting at P_i are collinear. Because every inserted positive-edge vertex lies strictly inside its sector, none equals P_i, so P_i lies in the relative interior of that straight join.

The four positive edges are exactly sectors `X_2,Y_1,X_3,X_1`. A strictly positive sector excess makes its inserted vertex a genuine strict turn: the turn determinant is `D_i(2W_i/D_i-1)>0`, up to the positive parametrization factors. The resulting replacement is therefore a quadrilateral with exactly those four vertices, and all six prescribed endpoints are on its edges.

## 3. Rigidity of every actual realizing body

Let K be any actual convex body realizing the same data. Choose an arbitrary actual supporting line of K at every P_i. The support-preserving exact sector replacement theorem produces a feasible polygon retaining all six chosen lines and all sector areas. Section 2 makes that replacement the same unique quadrilateral P, independently of the chosen lines.

Since each P_i lies in the relative interior of a quadrilateral edge, its supporting line in P is unique. The chosen actual support of K must therefore be that edge line. The six retained lines include all four edge lines of P. Consequently K is contained in P. Their total areas agree, as the six sector areas agree. Two full-dimensional compact convex sets with one contained in the other and equal area are equal: any missing point outside the smaller closed set would, together with a small interior ball, produce a positive-area subset of the difference. Hence K=P.

This proves actual-body uniqueness and the asserted quadrilateral structure. It does not eliminate this remaining quadrilateral case, nor the cases with further saturated sectors.
